items.title: A New Ground Opens: Seven Names for the Same Stillness

items.zh: 已說有尋有伺等三。云何三摩呬多地？
items.en: The Ground with Applied and Sustained Thought, and the two grounds following it, have now been fully explained. What is the Ground of Meditative Equipoise?

items.zh: 嗢拕南曰：總標、與安立、作意、相差別、攝諸經宗要、最後眾雜義。若略說三摩呬多地，當知由總標故，安立故，作意差別故，相差別故，略攝諸經宗要等故。云何總標？

items.title: Four Doors Named: Solitude, Stillness, Renouncing Joy, and Purified Equanimity

items.zh: 謂此地中略有四種。一者、靜慮，二者、解脫，三者、等持，四者、等至。靜慮者，謂四靜慮。一、從離生有尋有伺靜慮，二、從定生無尋無伺靜慮，三、離喜靜慮，四、捨念清淨靜慮。
items.en: Briefly, this ground has four parts: first, the meditative absorptions; second, the liberations; third, unifications; fourth, attainments. The meditative absorptions are the four dhyānas. First, the dhyāna with applied and sustained thought, arising from seclusion. Second, the dhyāna free of applied and sustained thought, arising from settled concentration. Third, the dhyāna of renouncing joy. Fourth, the dhyāna of purified equanimity and mindfulness.

items.title: Eight Liberations: Using Ugliness, Then Beauty, to Break the Same Attachment Two Ways

items.zh: 解脫者，謂八解脫。一、有色觀諸色解脫，二、內無色想觀外諸色解脫，三、淨解脫身作證具足住解脫，四、空無邊處解脫，五、識無邊處解脫，六、無所有處解脫，七、非想非非想處解脫，八、想受滅身作證具足住解脫。
items.en: The liberations are the eight liberations. First, liberation through contemplating forms while still perceiving form. Second, liberation through contemplating outward forms while no longer perceiving form inwardly. Third, liberation through the pure absorption directly realised and fully dwelt in. Fourth, liberation of the sphere of limitless space. Fifth, liberation of the sphere of limitless consciousness. Sixth, liberation of the sphere of nothing whatsoever. Seventh, liberation of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Eighth, liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling, directly realised and fully dwelt in.

items.title: Eleven Kinds of Unification, Six Kinds of Attainment — the Opening Outline Closes

items.zh: 等持者，謂三三摩地。一、空，二、無願，三、無相。復有三種。謂有尋有伺、無尋唯伺、無尋無伺。復有三種。謂小、大、無量。復有二種。謂一分修、具分修。復有三種。謂喜俱行、樂俱行、捨俱行。復有四種。謂四修定。復有五種。謂五聖智三摩地。復有五種。謂聖五支三摩地。復有有因有具聖正三摩地。復有金剛喻三摩地。復有有學、無學、非學非無學等三摩地。
items.en: Unification is the three concentrations: emptiness, aimlessness, and signlessness. There are, further, three more: with applied and sustained thought, without applied thought but with sustained thought alone, and without either. There are, further, three more: small, great, and immeasurable. There are, further, two more: cultivated only in part, and cultivated in full. There are, further, three more: accompanied by joy, by bliss, and by equanimity. There are, further, four more: the four cultivations of concentration. There are, further, five more: the five concentrations of noble wisdom. There are, further, five more: the five noble limbs of concentration. There is, further, the noble right concentration that has both a cause and its full equipment. There is, further, the vajra-like concentration. There are, further, three more: belonging to one still in training, to one beyond training, and to neither.

items.zh: 等至者，謂五現見三摩鉢底、八勝處三摩鉢底、十遍處三摩鉢底、四無色三摩鉢底、無想三摩鉢底、滅盡定等三摩鉢底。
items.en: Attainment is the directly-observed attainments, the attainments of the eight forms of mastery, the attainments of the ten totality-spheres, the four formless attainments, the attainment without perception, and the attainment of cessation, among others.

items.title: What Actually Makes a State of Mind "Equipoise": Not Desire-Realm Focus, But No-Regret's Whole Causal Chain

items.zh: 謂唯此等名等引地，非於欲界心一境性。由此定等無悔、歡喜、安樂所引；欲界不爾。非欲界中於法全無審正觀察。
items.en: Only these — the meditative absorptions, liberations, unifications, and attainments just named — are called the Ground of Meditative Equipoise; the desire realm's own one-pointedness of mind is not. This is because these states of concentration are drawn forth by freedom from regret, by joy, and by ease of body and mind; the desire realm's one-pointedness is not drawn forth this way — though it is not the case that the desire realm is entirely without careful, correct examination of things.

items.title: Five Things the First Dhyāna Abandons, Including a King Who Lets His Servants Do Wrong

items.zh: 復次，初靜慮中說離生喜，由證住此，斷除五法。謂欲所引喜、欲所引憂、不善所引喜、不善所引憂、不善所引捨。又於五法修習圓滿。謂歡、喜、安、樂、及三摩地。欲所引喜者，於妙五欲若初得時、若已證得正受用時，或見、或聞、或曾領受；由此諸緣，憶念歡喜。欲所引憂者，於妙五欲若求不遂，若已受用更不復得，或得已便失；由此諸緣，多生憂惱。
items.en: Further, in the first dhyāna, called "joy arisen from seclusion," one who has realised and settled into it abandons five things: joy induced by desire, sorrow induced by desire, joy induced by wrongdoing, sorrow induced by wrongdoing, and equanimity induced by wrongdoing. Joy induced by desire is this: when first obtaining an attractive sensory pleasure, or actually experiencing it, or having seen it, heard it, or otherwise experienced it — recalling any of these, joy arises. Sorrow induced by desire is this: seeking an attractive sensory pleasure and failing to obtain it, or having once enjoyed it and no longer being able to, or obtaining it and then losing it — from any of these, sorrow repeatedly arises.

items.zh: 不善所引喜者，謂如有一，與喜樂俱而行殺業，乃至邪見。不善所引憂者，謂如有一，與憂苦俱而行殺業，乃至邪見。不善所引捨者，謂如有一，或王、王等、或餘宰官、或尊、尊等，自不樂為殺等惡業，然其僕使作惡業時，忍而不制，亦不安處毘奈耶中，由縱捨故，遂造惡業。
items.en: Joy induced by wrongdoing is this: someone who commits killing or any of the other unwholesome deeds, up through wrong view, with joy and pleasure. Sorrow induced by wrongdoing is this: someone who commits killing or the rest with sorrow and distress. Equanimity induced by wrongdoing is this: a king, or one of equal standing, or some other official or dignitary, who does not personally delight in killing or other wrongdoing, yet who witnesses a servant committing wrongdoing and tolerates it without restraining them, neither placing them under proper discipline — through this very indulgence, wrongdoing is thereby committed, and this person is well aware of it, not unaware.

items.zh: 彼於此業現前領解，非不現前。
又住於捨，尋求伺察為惡方便。又於諸惡耽著不斷，引發於捨。又於不善現前轉時，發起中庸非苦樂受。
items.en: Further, resting in this indulgent equanimity, one applies coarse and subtle thought towards devising ways to do wrong. Further, indulging in wrongdoing without ever severing it, one's habitual disposition itself gives rise to this equanimity. Further, at the very moment wrongdoing occurs, a neutral feeling arises, neither painful nor pleasant.

items.title: Five Things Cultivated: Gladness, Joy, Tranquility, Bliss, and One-Pointedness

items.zh: 歡者，謂從本來清淨行者，觀資糧地所修淨行，無悔為先，慰意適悅，心欣踊性。喜者，謂正修習方便為先，深慶適悅、心欣踊性。
items.en: Further, five qualities are brought to full completion: gladness, joy, tranquility, bliss, and concentration. Gladness is this: a practitioner of consistently pure conduct, reflecting on the pure practices cultivated at the stage of gathering the provisions for practice, finds no grounds for regret, and from this arises a settled comfort and contentment, the mind's own genuine delight. Joy is this: grounded first in genuinely undertaking the actual practice of meditation itself, a profound gladness and contentment arises, the mind's own delight rising still further.

items.zh: 安者，謂離麁重，身心調適性。樂者，謂由如是心調適故，便得身心無損害樂及解脫樂；以離彼品麁重性故，於諸煩惱而得解脫。三摩地者，謂於所緣審正觀察，心一境性。
items.en: Tranquility is this: once coarse unfitness is left behind, body and mind become genuinely well-adapted and at ease. Bliss is this: because the mind has become so well-adapted, one obtains both an unharmed bodily and mental bliss and the bliss of genuine release — and, by leaving behind that same coarse unfitness, one is freed from the afflictions it sustained. Concentration is this: careful, correct observation resting on one single object, the mind's own one-pointedness.

items.title: Why the Buddha Teaches Concentration Before Liberation

items.zh: 世尊於無漏方便中，先說三摩地，後說解脫。由三摩地善成滿力，於諸煩惱心永解脫故。
items.en: Within the uncontaminated method, the Blessed One teaches concentration first and liberation second — because it is precisely through the accomplished power of concentration, brought to full completion, that the mind becomes forever liberated from the afflictions.

blocks.text: With fascicle 11 we reach the sixth of the seventeen stages, the **Stage of Meditative Absorption** (三摩呬多地, *samāhitā bhūmiḥ*). After ten fascicles describing the mind and how it binds itself, the treatise turns to how it is trained. This stage is the treatise's manual of concentration. Venerable Miào Jìng's lectures on it are especially practical; he had taught meditation for decades.

The stage opens with names: **dhyāna** (靜慮), **liberation** (解脫), **concentration** (等持, *samādhi*), **attainment** (等至, *samāpatti*), and **equipoise** (等引, *samāhita*). Master Cháng Bǎi: 等引 is the broadest. Among them, the four dhyānas are especially suited to noble ones, because they balance calm and wisdom; the formless attainments are strong in calm but weak in wisdom.

The four **dhyānas**: the first, with applied and sustained thought, "arising from solitude" (Master Cháng Bǎi: separation from desire, ill will, and harm; "solitude" understates it); the second, without thought, arising from concentration; the third, renouncing joy; the fourth, with purified equanimity and mindfulness. Master Cháng Bǎi on the last step: one sees the fault even in the third dhyāna's bliss, "not wanting to be disturbed even by pleasure", and lets it go.

subs.head: Eight liberations, and kinds of concentration

blocks.text: The **eight liberations** (八解脫) are eight progressively deeper meditations that cut the afflictions of the three realms. Master Cháng Bǎi: they use the perception of unattractiveness and then of beauty to break the same attachment in two ways; the third dhyāna is not used as a basis because, being the most blissful state in the three realms, impurity contemplation is hard there.

The concentrations include the three **gateways of liberation**: emptiness, aimlessness, and signlessness; the "five noble limbs" (the four dhyānas and the concentration that investigates dependent origination); and the "four cultivations": for happiness here and now, for knowledge and vision, for discriminating wisdom, and for ending the outflows.

Why is desire-realm one-pointedness not "equipoise"? Because true concentration is "drawn forth by freedom from regret, by joy, and by ease of body and mind", which the desire realm lacks. Venerable Miào Jìng adds, citing the *Satyasiddhi*, that even desire-realm concentration can support attaining the path, with less force.
The causal chain is worth memorising: pure conduct → no regret → gladness → joy → tranquillity → bliss → concentration. It begins with ethics.

subs.head: What the first dhyāna abandons and cultivates

blocks.text: The first dhyāna abandons five things, including "equanimity induced by wrongdoing": like a king who does not like wrongdoing himself but lets his servants do it unchecked. Venerable Miào Jìng: indulgence in others' wrongdoing is itself a fault the meditator must abandon.

It cultivates five: **gladness**, **joy**, **tranquillity**, **bliss**, and **one-pointedness**. Venerable Miào Jìng: gladness comes in preparation ("I've made no mistakes, my precepts are pure, all conditions are ready"), joy in actual practice.

"Within the uncontaminated method, the Blessed One teaches concentration first and liberation second." Venerable Miào Jìng: "Without concentration your mind is scattered; practising the foundations of mindfulness won't work; it can't cut afflictions." In the worldly method the order is reversed, and its "liberation" is temporary. Master Cháng Bǎi: like grass pressed under a stone, afflictions are held down, not uprooted.

quiz.q: Which of the seventeen grounds is the Ground of Meditative Equipoise, according to Venerable Miào Jìng?
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The Basic Section has seventeen grounds; this is the sixth, the Ground of Meditative Equipoise." Fascicles 4–10 covered the three grounds with applied and sustained thought (the third to fifth).

quiz.q: Which list correctly names the four dhyānas?
options: arising from solitude with thought; arising from concentration without thought; renouncing joy; purified equanimity and mindfulness
quiz.why: "First, the dhyāna with applied and sustained thought, arising from solitude. Second, the dhyāna free of applied and sustained thought, arising from settled concentration. Third, the dhyāna of renouncing joy. Fourth, the dhyāna of purified equanimity and mindfulness." Master Cháng Bǎi: the first is "born of separation" from desire, ill will, and harm.

quiz.q: How does one enter the fourth dhyāna, according to Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: see the fault in the third dhyāna's bliss, not wanting to be disturbed even by pleasure, and let it go
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "One enters the fourth dhyāna by observing the fault in the third's bliss — finding even bliss undesirable, not wanting to be disturbed by it, one lets it go, attaining purified equanimity and mindfulness." §23: the fourth dhyāna, seeing bliss's fault, is "stilled of bliss."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the three concentrations among the unifications?
quiz.why: "Unification is the three concentrations: emptiness, aimlessness, and signlessness." Venerable Miào Jìng: aimlessness sits between emptiness and signlessness for a reason. Eleven classifications of unification follow.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why isn't the desire realm's one-pointedness called the Ground of Equipoise?
options: concentration is drawn forth by no-regret, joy, and ease, which desire-realm focus lacks — though it isn't wholly without careful examination
quiz.why: "These states of concentration are drawn forth by freedom from regret, by joy, and by ease of body and mind; the desire realm's one-pointedness is not … though it is not the case that the desire realm is entirely without careful, correct examination of things." Venerable Miào Jìng: its skill is too shallow, but its examining power isn't denied.

quiz.q: Among the five qualities perfected, how do 歡 (gladness) and 喜 (joy) differ, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: gladness comes in preparation — pure precepts and conditions ready; joy comes in actual practice
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Gladness is at the preparation stage — I've made no mistakes, precepts pure, all conditions well prepared, so the heart is glad." The text: gladness comes from reviewing pure conduct without regret; joy from actually practising.

quiz.q: Why, in the uncontaminated method, does the Buddha teach concentration first?
options: through concentration's accomplished power, the mind is forever freed from afflictions
quiz.why: "Within the uncontaminated method, the Blessed One teaches concentration first and liberation second — because it is precisely through the accomplished power of concentration … that the mind becomes forever liberated." Master Cháng Bǎi: best to rely on the seven root absorptions (excluding the peak).
